theory.title: Understanding Test Cases and the Log Keyword
theory.content:
You wake up in the damaged ship. MENTOR-9's voice is calm but urgent.

"PROTO-7, our ship's diagnostic system needs to verify you're functional. Use the Log protocol—it's how we robots communicate with test systems."

What is a Test Case?

In Robot Framework, a test case is a named sequence of actions (keywords) that verify some behavior. Think of it like a checklist:

  • Each test case has a name
  • Below the name, you write the steps (keywords) to execute
  • If all steps succeed, the test passes ✅
  • If any step fails, the test fails ❌

The Basic Structure

Every Robot Framework file has sections marked by ***. Here's your first test:

*** Test Cases ***
My Test Name
    Log    Hello World

⚠️ Critical Spacing Rules

  • Test names start at the left (no indentation)
  • Keywords must be indented with at least 2 spaces (4 spaces recommended for readability)
  • Separate keywords and arguments with at least 2 spaces (4 is standard)
  • Tabs can work but may cause issues with mixed editors—stick to spaces

Best practice: Use 4 spaces consistently throughout your test files!

Understanding Indentation

Robot Framework is whitespace-sensitive. The minimum requirements are:

  • Test case body: Minimum 2 spaces indentation (4 recommended)
  • Keyword/argument separation: Minimum 2 spaces (4 standard)

Valid examples:

*** Test Cases ***
Test With 2 Spaces
  Log  Message

Test With 4 Spaces
    Log    Message

Test With Tabs
	Log	Message

Notes on each style:

  • 2 spaces: Works but hard to read, not recommended
  • 4 spaces: Recommended standard, best readability
  • Tabs: Works but avoid due to editor inconsistencies

Why 4 spaces is the standard:

  • Better readability and visual hierarchy
  • Consistent across teams and projects
  • Matches Python's PEP 8 style guide
  • Avoids tab/space mixing issues

The Log Keyword

The Log keyword outputs messages to the test log file (log.html). It's your primary debugging tool.

Syntax:

Log    Your message here

Why Use Log?

  • Debugging: See what values variables have
  • Verification: Confirm code paths execute
  • Documentation: Add runtime notes to reports

MENTOR-9 nods. "Your turn, PROTO-7. Create a test case called 'Communication Test' and log the message 'System online'. Show me you can communicate."

theory.title: Sequential Keyword Execution
theory.content:
MENTOR-9 brings up a holographic display. "PROTO-7, test automation isn't about single actions—it's about sequences of actions that represent complete workflows."

Multi-Step Tests

Robot Framework executes keywords sequentially from top to bottom. Each line represents one action:

*** Test Cases ***
Ship Diagnostic
    Log    Starting diagnostic...
    Log    Checking hull integrity
    Log    Checking power systems
    Log    Diagnostic complete

Execution Order

  1. Robot Framework finds the *** Test Cases *** section
  2. It identifies your test case by name
  3. It executes each indented keyword line by line
  4. If all keywords succeed, the test passes
  5. If any keyword fails, the test stops and fails

Why Sequential Execution Matters

Order matters! You can't verify a welcome message before logging in. You can't check engine temperature before starting the engine.

Sequential execution makes tests read like documentation—anyone can understand what the test does by reading top to bottom.

MENTOR-9: "Now send me a status report with three messages. Tell me about the hull, power, and communication systems. Show me you can build workflows."

story.success: MENTOR-9: "Perfect format. If any rescue ships are nearby, they'll understand that signal."

Create a test case named 'Emergency Signal'
Log the exact message: 'DISTRESS: Ship Starlight Explorer requesting assistance'

Test case name on next line, no indentation

theory.title: Working with Text in Log Messages
theory.content:
MENTOR-9's sensors detect something. "PROTO-7, I'm picking up faint radio signals. Other ships might be in range. We need to send a distress signal—but it must follow the proper format, or they won't recognize it."

Log Messages and Text

The Log keyword accepts any text as its argument. This includes:

  • Letters and numbers: System 42 online
  • Punctuation: Status: OK! Temperature: 98.6°C
  • Multiple words with spaces: This is a complete sentence
  • Special characters: Error: CPU@95% #CRITICAL

Do You Need Quotes?

Usually no. Robot Framework treats everything after the 4-space separator as the message:

Log    This entire line is the message
Log    "You can use quotes if you want"
Log    Both work the same way!

When quotes matter:

  • When using variables (covered later)
  • When passing multiple arguments to keywords
  • For now, you can write messages naturally without quotes

Message Formatting

Your messages should be:

  • Clear: "Starting engine" not "SE"
  • Specific: "Temperature: 42°C" not "Temp ok"
  • Consistent: Pick a style and stick with it

MENTOR-9: "Send the standard distress signal. Format matters—other ships will ignore malformed messages. The signal must be: 'DISTRESS: Ship Starlight Explorer requesting assistance'"

exercises.title: Log Levels
exercises.description: Use different log levels to indicate message severity.

story.setup: MENTOR-9: "Not all messages are equal. Some are informational, some are warnings, some are critical errors. We use log levels to indicate severity."
story.context: The Log keyword accepts an optional second argument: the log level (INFO, WARN, ERROR).
story.success: MENTOR-9: "Good! Now anyone reading the logs will immediately see which issues need urgent attention."

instructions: Create the *** Test Cases *** section
Create a test case named 'System Analysis'
Log 'Navigation operational' at INFO level
Log 'Hull breach detected in sector 7' at WARN level
Log 'Life support failure imminent' at ERROR level
hints: Start with *** Test Cases *** header
Syntax for log levels: Log    message    LEVEL
Valid levels: INFO, WARN, ERROR (uppercase)
INFO is the default if no level is specified
The level comes AFTER the message, separated by spaces

*** Test Cases ***
System Analysis
    Log    Navigation operational    INFO
    Log    Hull breach detected in sector 7    WARN
    Log    Life support failure imminent    ERROR

theory.title: Log Levels and Message Severity
theory.content:
MENTOR-9 pulls up the ship's log display. It's cluttered with hundreds of messages—all appearing equally important.

"This is chaos, PROTO-7. We need to prioritize. That's where log levels come in."

What Are Log Levels?

Log levels indicate the severity or importance of a message. Robot Framework supports several levels:

LevelUsageExample
INFONormal operational messages"User logged in successfully"
WARNPotential issues, non-critical"API response slow (3.2s)"
ERRORErrors that don't stop the test"Database connection timeout"
DEBUGDetailed debugging info"Variable value: ${x} = 42"
TRACEVery detailed debugging"Entering loop iteration 5"

Syntax

Log    Normal message
Log    Normal message    INFO
Log    Warning message   WARN
Log    Error occurred    ERROR

Notes:

  • First line: No level specified = INFO by default
  • Second line: INFO explicitly stated
  • Third line: WARN level for warnings
  • Fourth line: ERROR level for errors

When to Use Each Level

  • INFO: Standard progress updates ("Starting test", "Page loaded")
  • WARN: Things that aren't quite right but test continues ("Slow response", "Deprecated API")
  • ERROR: Problems that might cause issues ("Connection failed", "Element not found")

Visual Impact

In the HTML log report:

  • INFO messages appear in black
  • WARN messages appear in orange
  • ERROR messages appear in red

This makes critical issues immediately visible!

MENTOR-9: "Analyze our ship systems. Log 'Navigation operational' as INFO, 'Hull breach in sector 7' as WARN, and 'Life support failure imminent' as ERROR. Let's see the severity clearly."

exercises.title: Console Output
exercises.description: Learn the difference between Log and Log To Console.

story.setup: MENTOR-9: "The Log keyword writes to the HTML report. But sometimes you want immediate feedback in the console—especially during development."
story.context: Log To Console outputs directly to the terminal/console where tests are running.
story.success: MENTOR-9: "Perfect! Now you know when to use each: Log for reports, Log To Console for real-time feedback."

instructions: Create the *** Test Cases *** section
Create a test case named 'Dual Output'
Use Log to output 'Writing to log file'
Use Log To Console to output 'Writing to console'
hints: Start with *** Test Cases *** header
Log writes to log.html (visible after test completes)
Log To Console writes to the console (visible during test execution)
Both keywords use the same syntax: keyword    message
Note the keyword is 'Log To Console' (three words, spaces between)
exercises.solution:
*** Test Cases ***
Dual Output
    Log    Writing to log file
    Log To Console    Writing to console

theory.title: Log vs Log To Console: When to Use Each
theory.content:
MENTOR-9 taps a display. "PROTO-7, notice how you only see Log messages after opening the HTML report? Sometimes you need real-time feedback while tests run. That's where Log To Console comes in."

Two Output Destinations

Robot Framework has two main logging keywords:

KeywordOutputWhen VisibleUse Case
Log log.html report After test completes Permanent record, detailed debugging
Log To Console Terminal/console Immediately, during execution Real-time feedback, progress tracking

Examples

*** Test Cases ***
Progress Tracking
    Log To Console    Starting test suite...
    Log               Detailed step 1 info
    Log To Console    25% complete
    Log               Detailed step 2 info
    Log To Console    50% complete
    Log To Console    Test complete!

When to Use Log

  • Recording variable values for later analysis
  • Detailed debugging information
  • Creating an audit trail of test actions
  • Anything you want preserved in the HTML report

When to Use Log To Console

  • Progress updates for long-running tests
  • Quick checks during test development
  • CI/CD pipeline output (visible in build logs)
  • Immediate feedback without opening HTML reports

Pro Tip: Use Both!

It's common to use both in the same test:

Log To Console    Starting API test...
Log               Request URL: https://api.example.com
Log               Headers: ${headers}
${response}       GET  /users/1
Log               Response: ${response}
Log To Console    Test passed!

This gives you real-time progress in the console and detailed records in the HTML report.

MENTOR-9: "Try both. Log 'Writing to log file' and use Log To Console for 'Writing to console'. Watch where each message appears."
